lead: Attenuation is the loss of optical power as light travels down a fiber. It is quoted as a coefficient in dB per kilometre, because a receiver needs a minimum power and every kilometre takes a fixed share away. The coefficient decides how far a link can reach before an amplifier or repeater is needed. A 1550 nm long-haul system, a 1310 nm metro link and a short 850 nm data link all use the same arithmetic, which this chapter sets up for the whole unit.

blocks.text: Let P<sub>in</sub> be the optical power launched into a fiber of length L km, and P<sub>out</sub> the power that leaves the far end. Both powers use the same unit, for example mW or µW. The attenuation coefficient is the loss per kilometre:

α = (10/L) log₁₀(Pin/Pout)
α is the attenuation coefficient in dB/km; L is the fiber length in km; Pin and Pout are the input and output powers in the same unit; log₁₀ is the base-10 logarithm.
The loss over the whole length is A = αL in dB. To go the other way, P<sub>out</sub> = P<sub>in</sub> × 10<sup>−A/10</sup>, that is, P<sub>in</sub> times ten raised to the power −A/10.

Two anchor points make the decibel easy. A loss of 3 dB halves the power, because 10 log₁₀2 = 3.01 dB. A loss of 10 dB divides the power by ten, and 20 dB by a hundred. A 3 dB coupler is named this way because each of its two outputs carries half the input power, so each output port is 3 dB below the input.

Absolute power is quoted in dBm, decibels relative to 1 mW: P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW). So 1 mW is 0 dBm, 0.5 mW is −3 dBm and 1 µW is −30 dBm. A launch power in dBm minus the losses in dB gives the received power in dBm, with no multiplication at all.

sections.h3: Four loss families add in dB

blocks.text: Four families cover almost every loss in a fiber link. Each gives its own dB value, and the total loss is their sum.

items: Absorption: light turned into heat by the glass and its impurities (see absorption losses).
Scattering: light thrown out of the core by tiny index fluctuations (see Rayleigh and Mie scattering).
Bending: light that radiates out where the fiber is curved (see bending losses).
Joint loss: light lost where two fibers meet at a splice or connector (see fiber joints and connectors).

blocks.text:
Atotal = Aabs + Ascat + Abend + Ajoint
Atotal is the total loss in dB; each term on the right is that family’s loss in dB.

The fiber terms are usually lumped into one coefficient α in dB/km, and the joints are counted as so many dB each. The sum works because dB is logarithmic: powers multiply along the link, and the logarithm turns that product into a sum. Never add powers in mW and then convert; add the dB losses, then convert once. The full link power budget, with receiver sensitivity and margin, comes with link design.

sections.h3: Standard windows and the water peak

blocks.text: Silica fiber is not equally clear at all wavelengths. Three transmission windows are used. The table also lists the water peak, which is a loss feature to avoid, not a window.

Long-haul links work at 1550 nm because each kilometre costs the fewest dB, so the spacing between amplifiers is longest; erbium-doped fiber amplifiers also work in this band. Low-water-peak fiber removes most of the 1383 nm bump, so the whole 1260 to 1625 nm range becomes usable.

Some books write the coefficient in nepers. From P<sub>out</sub> = P<sub>in</sub>e<sup>−α′L</sup>, the neper coefficient α′ and the dB coefficient α are related by α = 4.343 α′, so α′ = 0.2303 α. A dB/km value times 0.2303 gives Np/km; divide that by 1000 for Np/m.

examples.question: A 1550 nm link uses fiber with α = 0.2 dB/km and launches 1 mW. (a) Find the loss over 80 km. (b) Find the power at the far end in dBm and in µW. (c) Find the length at which the power falls to 1 µW.
steps: Loss: A = αL = 0.2 dB/km × 80 km = 16 dB.
Launch power: 1 mW = 0 dBm, so the received power is 0 − 16 = −16 dBm.
In watts: P<sub>out</sub> = 1 mW × 10<sup>−16/10</sup> = 1 mW × 10<sup>−1.6</sup> = 1 mW × 0.0251 = 0.0251 mW = 25.1 µW.
For part (c), 1 µW is −30 dBm, so the allowed loss is 0 − (−30) = 30 dB.
examples.answer: 16 dB over 80 km; −16 dBm, which is 25.1 µW; the power reaches 1 µW after 150 km.

examples.question: A 6 km fiber is tested at 1310 nm. The launched power is 120 µW and the power at the far end is 36 µW. Find the attenuation coefficient, and give both powers in dBm.
steps: log₁₀ 3.333 = 0.5229, so the total loss is A = 10 × 0.5229 = 5.229 dB.
Coefficient: α = A/L = 5.229 dB ÷ 6 km = 0.871 dB/km.
In dBm: 120 µW = 0.120 mW gives 10 log₁₀ 0.120 = −9.21 dBm; 36 µW gives 10 log₁₀ 0.036 = −14.44 dBm.
Check: −9.21 − (−14.44) = 5.23 dB, the same loss as step 2.
examples.answer: α = 0.87 dB/km; the powers are −9.21 dBm in and −14.44 dBm out. A value this high at 1310 nm points to a cable with extra bend or joint loss, not to clean fiber.

traps: Writing A = α/L instead of A = αL. α is per kilometre, so multiplying by L km leaves dB.
Adding a dB/km coefficient to a dB loss. Multiply each coefficient by its length first, then add the dB values.
Adding powers in mW and then taking a logarithm. Losses add in dB; convert to mW only at the end.
A sign slip in the formula. With P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub> inside the logarithm the loss is positive; if you write P<sub>out</sub>/P<sub>in</sub> you get the same number with a minus sign.
Mixing dB and dBm. dB is a ratio (a loss or a gain); dBm is an absolute power. Received power in dBm = launch power in dBm − loss in dB.

quiz.q: Define the attenuation coefficient of an optical fiber and give its usual unit.
quiz.a: The loss per unit length, α = (10/L) log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>), with L in km, so α is in dB/km.

quiz.q: Why do we add losses in dB instead of adding powers in mW?
quiz.a: Each section passes a fraction of the power, so the fractions multiply: P<sub>out</sub> = P<sub>in</sub> × 10<sup>−A/10</sup>. Taking logarithms turns the product into a sum, so the dB losses add.

quiz.q: A fiber has α = 0.4 dB/km. Find the loss over 25 km and the output power if the input is 2 mW.
quiz.a: A = 0.4 × 25 = 10 dB. P<sub>out</sub> = 2 mW × 10<sup>−1</sup> = 0.2 mW (3 dBm − 10 dB = −7 dBm).

quiz.q: A link may lose 24 dB. If the fiber has α = 0.3 dB/km, what is the longest fiber allowed, ignoring joints?
A 1310 nm link uses 60 km of fiber with α = 0.35 dB/km and four connectors of 0.5 dB each. Find the total loss and the received power for a 0 dBm launch.
quiz.a: Fiber 0.35 × 60 = 21 dB; connectors 4 × 0.5 = 2 dB; total 23 dB. Received power 0 − 23 = −23 dBm, about 5 µW.

quiz.q: Why does 1550 nm give a longer unrepeated span than 850 nm for the same allowed loss? Use typical numbers.
quiz.a: For a fixed loss the length scales as 1/α. With 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm and 2.5 dB/km at 850 nm the span is 2.5/0.2 = 12.5 times longer, before dispersion limits are counted.

quiz.q: Convert α = 0.2 dB/km to nepers per metre.
quiz.a: 0.2 × 0.2303 = 0.0461 Np/km; divided by 1000 this is 4.61 × 10<sup>−5</sup> Np/m.

beyond: The 0.2 dB/km figure is for the fiber itself; installed cable adds splice and bend loss, and hydrogen ingress can raise loss over the years. Pure-silica-core fibers for submarine cables reach about 0.15 dB/km at 1550 nm. An optical time-domain reflectometer (OTDR) measures the loss of a fiber from one end by timing the light scattered back along it. Search next for “OTDR trace”, “low-water-peak fiber” and “optical power budget”.

figure.caption: On a dBm scale the power falls in a straight line, 0.2 dB for every kilometre at 1550 nm. The 1 mW launch is 25.1 µW (−16 dBm) after 80 km and reaches the 1 µW receiver limit at 150 km; at 0.35 dB/km (1310 nm) the same limit comes at 85.7 km.
